title: Keep the Voices Straight: Cross-Text Connections
description: Separate two texts’ claims, identify the exact relationship the question asks about, and prove agreement, difference, or a likely response using both texts.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first choice and what made it seem plausible. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Two accounts of a railway
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1
Basket sales in a mountain town rose sharply during the decade after its railway station opened. One historian explains the increase using shipping records: local makers could now send more goods to markets outside the valley. The records document baskets moving outward in growing quantities. The railway’s main contribution, the historian argues, was making distant buyers accessible to the town’s craftworkers.

Text 2
A second historian accepts that the railway helped the industry grow, but examines workshop diaries rather than shipping totals. The diaries record visitors arriving by train, buying baskets directly, and requesting shapes and patterns absent from earlier catalogs. Makers adopted some of those requests. The diaries do not establish whether local or distant purchases accounted for more sales, but they reveal customer contact that shipping figures do not capture.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

  1. By accepting the railway’s role in growth while adding that incoming visitors also helped shape the goods being made
  2. By accepting the railway’s role in growth while arguing that visiting buyers replaced distant markets as the industry’s main source of demand
  3. By accepting that visitors requested new designs while arguing that those requests reflected the preferences of buyers in distant markets
  4. By accepting the evidence of increased sales while arguing that the timing leaves the connection between growth and railway traffic uncertain

content.html:
Keep agreement separate from an added claim

The railway choices reuse facts from both texts, but they connect those facts differently. A response can accept one part of an account while adding something it misses.

We’ll use Keep the Voices Straight to state each writer’s view before connecting them. Start with two shorter views of a town square.

Find the shared claim

Read the two views of the benches. Name something both writers support, then name the limit the second writer adds.

content.hint: Find a claim with evidence in each text, not just a shared topic.
content.prompt: Which statement do both writers support?
choices: Shade would make the square useful even without adding benches.
The square received few visitors before the benches were installed.
The benches encourage people to linger.
The benches have made the square comfortable during hot weather.
content.solution: Text 1: people stop to talk. Text 2: people linger. These support the same claim, C. Text 2’s criticism of heat does not cancel that agreement.
content.explanation: Both describe people staying longer. Shade is Text 2’s addition; neither supplies a history of usage or a claim about every season.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1
The new benches in the square have made it a better place to spend time. More people stop there to talk instead of simply passing through.

Text 2
The benches have encouraged people to linger in the square. However, because none are shaded, they are difficult to use on hot afternoons. The next improvement should be shade.

content.html:
Name the connection

Agreement means both support a claim. Disagreement means their claims conflict. A qualification accepts part of a claim while adding a limit. “Yes, but” is different from “No.”

content.hint: Separate agreement about searching from the criticism about completeness.
content.prompt: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
choices: It accepts the improvement while pointing out a remaining limitation.
It rejects the claim that the catalog improves access to documents.
It explains why the archive’s documents are difficult to preserve.
It argues that the catalog lists documents that do not belong in the archive.
content.solution: Easier searching is shared ground. Missing documents limit the achievement rather than reverse it.
content.explanation: Easier searching is shared ground. Missing documents limit the achievement rather than reverse it.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: Text 1 says a new catalog makes an archive easier to search. Text 2 agrees that searching is easier but says the catalog still leaves many documents unlisted.

content.html:
Keep the Voices Straight

  1. Identify who responds to which claim.
  2. State each text’s view separately.
  3. Predict the connection.
  4. Check each part of the answer against the right text.

Predict a response

The critic says recordings preserve melodies, so they are enough. The folklorist says recordings help but miss practices and context. The response is “useful, but not enough by themselves.” That accepts the benefit while limiting the conclusion.

content.hint: Respond to sufficiency using the folklorist’s actual concern.
content.prompt: How would the folklorist most likely respond to the critic’s claim that recordings are sufficient?
choices: Recordings often distort the melodies that listeners hope to preserve.
Recordings preserve melodies but leave out meaningful context.
Future listeners may prefer newer music to traditional songs.
Recordings are more useful than teaching songs in person.
content.solution: Locate “sufficient” in Text 1. Apply Text 2’s distinction between melody and social practice. B preserves both the usefulness of recordings and their limitation.
content.explanation: Text 2 values recordings and identifies what they omit. It neither rejects their accuracy nor predicts future listeners’ interest.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1
A music critic argues that recordings are sufficient for preserving a local song tradition. They retain the melodies accurately, allowing future listeners to hear songs that might otherwise disappear.

Text 2
A folklorist values recordings but notes that a song tradition includes more than melody. The occasions when people sing, and the ways they teach songs to one another, also carry meaning that a recording alone may not capture.

content.html:
Check who is responding

If the question asks how Text 1 would respond, use Text 1’s view. The order of the boxes does not decide the direction. Keep the responding writer in mind before you read the choices.

content.hint: The responder is the curator. Use the benefit that the curator actually names.
content.prompt: How would the curator in Text 1 most likely respond to the critic?
choices: Replicas should be removed because they distract visitors from original objects.
Visitors often confuse replicas with the original objects they represent.
Original objects offer fewer signs of wear than the critic suggests.
Replicas allow handling while protecting originals.
content.solution: Identify the responding voice: curator. Retrieve that voice’s reason: handling replicas protects originals. Apply it to the criticism; D offers the stated benefit rather than inventing a denial.
content.explanation: The curator’s stated reason is access without damage. D uses that position without pretending to disprove the critic’s point.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1: A curator argues that replicas let visitors handle objects without damaging the originals.

Text 2: A critic argues that a replica cannot convey the marks left by centuries of use.

content.html:
Respond to the exact claim

A writer may report another person’s view and then question it. Keep the speaker attached to each claim. If the question quotes one claim, compare that claim with the other text.

content.hint: The question targets the historians’ explanation, not Text 1’s later objection.
content.prompt: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historians’ claim reported in Text 1?
choices: Safety concerns explain the closure despite audience interest.
The theater’s limited audience caused concern long before the closure.
Declining ticket sales explain why officials closed the building.
Records written after closure provide weak evidence of earlier conditions.
content.solution: Identify the quoted explanation: declining interest. Text 2 supplies a different possible reason and states that an audience remained. That supports the challenge in A.
content.explanation: Safety records and an audience that remained substantial undermine the declining-interest explanation. The records precede the closure.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1: Some historians argue that the theater closed because local interest declined. The author notes, however, that ticket sales were steady during its final year.

Text 2: Building records show that the theater was declared unsafe shortly before it closed, although its audience remained substantial.

content.html:
A result and its explanation can differ

A writer can accept that scores rose while questioning whether a new program caused the rise. Separate the observed result from the conclusion someone draws from it.

content.hint: Check whether Text 2 rejects the recorded change or the explanation for it.
content.prompt: Which choice best describes the relationship between the texts?
choices: Text 2 proves that longer hours caused the entire increase in borrowing.
Text 2 disputes whether the records show any increase in borrowing.
Text 2 accepts the increase but questions whether the club alone explains it.
Text 2 agrees that the club’s effect can be isolated from the records.
content.solution: Separate result from conclusion in Text 1. Text 2 calls the increase encouraging but introduces simultaneous longer hours. C captures the limited challenge.
content.explanation: Text 2 questions attribution, not the increase itself. It raises another explanation without establishing that explanation as the sole cause.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1: After a school introduced a reading club, participants borrowed more books. The organizer concludes that the club caused the increase.

Text 2: The borrowing increase is encouraging. However, the school extended library hours at the same time, so the records alone cannot show which change produced the increase.

content.html:
Agreement needs support from both texts

Test the proposed claim once against each writer. Sharing a topic does not mean sharing a belief. Keep only the claim both texts support.

content.hint: Look for the common limit on what a translation can preserve.
content.prompt:
Text 1: Translating a poem requires choices because a single phrase may combine sound and meaning in ways another language cannot reproduce exactly.

Text 2: A useful translation preserves a poem’s central images, even if doing so requires changing its rhythm. No version can retain every feature of the original.

Both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Preserving rhythm matters more than preserving a poem’s images.
An effective translation reproduces both the original rhythm and its wording.
Reading a poem in its original language is preferable to reading a translation.
Translating poetry requires tradeoffs.
content.solution: Text 1 says sound and meaning cannot always be reproduced exactly. Text 2 says no version retains every feature. Both support the tradeoffs in D.
content.explanation: Both describe an inability to preserve everything at once. Only Text 2 gives a specific priority, and neither tells readers what languages to study.

content.html:
Check both halves of a difference

An answer may say that Text 1 emphasizes one thing while Text 2 emphasizes another. Check each half separately. Different emphases do not always amount to disagreement.

Make one final speaker check

Ask who believes the claim, what issue it addresses, and how strongly the writer states it. A familiar idea attributed to the wrong writer still fails.

blocks.html:
Return to the two historians

Try the opening question again. State the views separately, then decide how the second writer would respond to the targeted claim.

content.prompt: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
choices: By accepting the railway’s role in growth while adding that incoming visitors also helped shape the goods being made
By accepting the railway’s role in growth while arguing that visiting buyers replaced distant markets as the industry’s main source of demand
By accepting that visitors requested new designs while arguing that those requests reflected the preferences of buyers in distant markets
By accepting the evidence of increased sales while arguing that the timing leaves the connection between growth and railway traffic uncertain
content.hint: Separate what Text 2 accepts from what its diary evidence adds. Do not turn an additional effect into a claim about which market mattered most.
content.solution:
Text 1 emphasizes access to distant buyers. Text 2 accepts railway-related growth and describes visiting customers’ requests for new designs.
The connection is an added dimension: customer contact affected production as well as sales opportunities.
Check both halves of each response against Text 2, including how strongly it treats the evidence.
Choose A.
B: The visitors are real, but Text 2 explicitly says the diaries do not establish which market produced more sales.
C: This borrows designs from Text 2 and distant markets from Text 1, but invents a connection between those buyers and the visitors’ requests.
D: Text 2 accepts the railway’s contribution; it adds a dimension rather than questioning that connection.
content.explanation: You kept the voices straight. The response adds an effect on what makers produced without inventing a winner between local and distant markets.

content.prompt: Two texts are on screen, and the question asks how one writer would respond to a specific claim. What is your first job in Keep the Voices Straight?
choices: Choose the answer that best summarizes the longer passage, then check the other passage.
Assume the second writer disagrees, then choose the strongest objection in the answer set.
Combine both texts into one opinion, then search for the choice with matching vocabulary.
Identify the responding writer and the exact claim, then connect that writer’s position to it.
content.explanation: Fix the direction and target first. Then separate the claims, predict the connection, and verify it against both texts.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: Which choice best describes a difference between the reviewers’ views?
choices: Text 1 values the plot’s speed, whereas Text 2 values the absence of repeated scenes.
Text 1 emphasizes what repetition reveals, whereas Text 2 emphasizes its cost to the pace.
Text 1 denies that the scenes repeat, whereas Text 2 argues that they repeat too often.
Text 1 favors a single narrator, whereas Text 2 favors several different narrators.
content.explanation: Both recognize repetition and differing perspectives. Their emphasis differs: added insight versus slower momentum.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1: A reviewer praises a novel’s repeated scenes because each retelling reveals a new character’s perspective.

Text 2: Another reviewer acknowledges the different perspectives but argues that the repetitions slow the novel’s momentum.

content.prompt: How would the researcher in Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
choices: The sites’ designs differ more than the first researcher suggests.
Similar designs can have different manufacturing origins.
Local clay sources became unavailable as the design spread.
Direct contact between the communities is unlikely given their distance.
content.explanation: Text 2 distinguishes shared appearance from shared manufacture. Local clay is evidence against the single-center inference, not against design similarity or communication.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html:
Text 1: An archaeologist argues that identical pottery designs at distant sites show that the vessels came from one production center.

Text 2: A researcher finds that the clay in those vessels comes from several local sources. Potters may have shared designs while making vessels locally.

content.html:
Keep the Voices Straight

Two claims first. Their connection second.
